title: An exponential separation between entanglement-assisted and unassisted one-way quantum communication
authors: Ryan Anselm, Srijita Kundu, Olivier Lalonde, Ashwin Nayak
abstract: A longstanding question in quantum communication complexity is whether some task can be accomplished with a small amount of communication in the presence of entanglement, yet require much more quantum communication in the absence of entanglement. Separations of this nature were previously known for relational problems and, in the simultaneous message passing model, for partial functions. But it has remained unresolved whether any such separation exists for a total Boolean function. We resolve this question with an exponential separation in the one-way setting: we exhibit a family of total Boolean functions $f_n\colon \{0,1\}^n \times \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ that can be computed with $O(\log n)$ bits of one-way classical communication given prior entanglement, but that require $Ω(n^{1/3})$ qubits of one-way quantum communication without entanglement. Our function is a special case of the subgroup membership problem, first studied in the communication setting by Aaronson, Le Gall, Russell, and Tani.
summary: This paper resolves a long-standing open problem by proving an exponential separation in the one-way quantum communication setting. They demonstrate that certain total Boolean functions can be computed using very few classical bits if entanglement is shared, but require significantly more quantum qubits if entanglement is unavailable. This result highlights the computational advantage of entanglement for total functions.
main_problem: The paper addresses the open question of whether an exponential separation exists between the communication complexity required for a total Boolean function when entanglement is available versus when it is not, specifically in the one-way communication setting.
main_result: The authors establish an exponential separation by constructing a family of total Boolean functions $f_n$ that require only $O(\log n)$ bits of one-way classical communication with prior entanglement, but $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ qubits without entanglement.
method: The proof involves establishing upper and lower bounds on the communication complexity for the function, utilizing techniques from quantum communication complexity theory and relating the problem to the subgroup membership problem.
model_or_system: The model is the one-way quantum communication setting for computing a total Boolean function $f_n: \{0, 1\}^n 	imes \{0, 1\}^n 	o \{0, 1\}$, comparing protocols that use shared entanglement versus those that do not.
key_observables: Communication cost (bits vs. qubits), success probability, and the separation gap (exponential vs. polynomial).
important_parameters: The function size $n$, the communication complexity bounds ($O(\log n)$ vs. $\Omega(n^{1/3})$), and the error tolerance ($\le 1/3$).
main_assumptions: The result holds for a family of total Boolean functions, and the lower bound techniques rely on specific mathematical principles like Yao's min-max principle.
paper_structure: The paper first frames the open question regarding total Boolean functions. It then establishes the upper bound using entanglement-assisted protocols (related to subgroup membership) and derives the lower bound for the unassisted quantum setting, culminating in the proof of the exponential separation.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, quantifiable separation in quantum communication complexity, which is a fundamental theoretical tool used to understand the power of entanglement in computation, relevant to quantum networking and information theory.
